questions.prompt: An image is 1280×720 and blocks are 32×8 threads. How many blocks does the grid need in total?
questions.explanation: ⌈1280/32⌉ = 40 by ⌈720/8⌉ = 90, so 40 × 90 = 3,600 blocks (no overhang: both divide exactly).

questions.prompt: Blocks are 16×16 and the thread has blockIdx = (3, 2) and threadIdx = (5, 9). What is its global y coordinate?
An RGB image is 640 pixels wide, row-major, 3 bytes per pixel. At what byte index is the green channel (c = 1) of pixel (x = 10, y = 2)?
Why does a 2D kernel need if (x < width && y < height)?
options: Because the grid is rounded up to whole blocks in each dimension, so some threads fall outside the image
questions.explanation: Rounding up in x and y creates threads past the right and bottom edges.

questions.prompt: Which are advantages of a grid-stride loop?
options: Correct for any n with any grid size
Launch size can match the machine instead of the data
Per-thread setup is paid once per thread, not per element
It removes the need for coalesced memory access
questions.explanation: Access pattern still matters. Grid-stride loops keep neighbouring threads on neighbouring elements, which helps, but they don't make coalescing irrelevant.

questions.prompt: In a grid-stride loop with 4 blocks of 256 threads, which elements does the thread with global index 5 process?
questions.explanation: The stride is the total thread count, 4 × 256 = 1,024, so 5, 1029, 2053, …
